paper_title: What Is Redundant at High Resolution? Efficient Attention and Feed-Forward Design for All-in-One Image Restoration

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multi-scale architectures are widely adopted in all-in-one image restoration (AIO-IR) to capture larger-scale context at low-resolution stages and refine details at high-resolution (HR) stages. However, processing spatially large feature maps at HR stages incurs substantial computational costs and memory traffic, making efficient HR processing challenging. To address this challenge, we propose High-resolution Global-Local Restoration (HiGLR), an efficient multi-scale AIO-IR network grounded in an analysis of spatial redundancy in self-attention and convolutional feed-forward networks (ConvFFNs). Specifically, this analysis identifies three key redundancies: per-query readout at the finest-scale stage, key routing across neighboring queries at intermediate stages, and spatial mixing in the expanded feature spaces of ConvFFNs. Accordingly, HiGLR replaces costly self-attention at the finest-scale stage with a learned input-independent kernel. At intermediate stages, we propose a Block-Routed Hybrid Attention, which combines coarse-scale dense attention with fine-scale block-sparse attention over value residuals relative to coarse summaries, and shares routing indices across neighboring queries. We further introduce a Dual-Space FFN that performs spatial mixing in a compact space and pointwise nonlinear transformation in an expanded space, enabling efficient kernel fusion. Combining these designs, HiGLR achieves state-of-the-art performance while delivering up to a $4.24\times$ inference speedup over existing methods.

sections.content: Multi-scale architectures are widely adopted in all-in-one image restoration (AIO-IR) to capture larger-scale context at low-resolution stages and refine details at highresolution (HR) stages. However, processing spatially large feature maps at HR stages incurs substantial computational costs and memory traffic, making efficient HR processing challenging. To address this challenge, we propose Highresolution Global-Local Restoration (HiGLR), an efficient multi-scale AIO-IR network grounded in an analysis of spatial redundancy in self-attention and convolutional feedforward networks (ConvFFNs). Specifically, this analysis identifies three key redundancies: per-query readout at the finest-scale stage, key routing across neighboring queries at intermediate stages, and spatial mixing in the expanded feature spaces of ConvFFNs. Accordingly, HiGLR replaces costly self-attention at the finest-scale stage with learned input-independent kernel. At intermediate stages, we propose Block-Routed Hybrid Attention, which combines coarse-scale dense attention with fine-scale block-sparse attention over value residuals relative to coarse summaries, and shares routing indices across neighboring queries. We further introduce Dual-Space FFN that performs spatial mixing in compact space and pointwise nonlinear transformation in an expanded space, enabling efficient kernel fusion. Combining these designs, HiGLR achieves state-ofthe-art performance while delivering up to 4.24 inference speedup over existing methods. [Code on GitHub] 1. Introduction Image restoration (IR) aims to recover high-quality images from degraded observations, including noise, blur, and haze [30, 39, 42]. Unlike conventional methods developed for individual degradations, all-in-one image restoration (AIO-IR) seeks to address diverse degradations using single unified model [12, 18, 25, 33, 38]. To restore images under such varied conditions, the model should utilize both broad contextual information and fine-grained spatial cues [39, 40]. Accordingly, U-Net [29]-like multi- *This work was done during an internship at NAVER Cloud. Co-corresponding authors. Figure 1. Comparisons of performance and inference latency on CDD-11. HiGLR achieves higher PSNR across all 11 degradation types with substantially lower latency. scale encoderdecoder architectures are widely used in AIO-IR [25, 28, 29, 38], integrating large-scale context with fine-grained spatial details across hierarchical highresolution (HR) and low-resolution (LR) stages. However, HR features are costly to process because of their large spatial dimensions. For example, spatial selfattention scales quadratically with the number of tokens, making it expensive at HR stages. While transposed attention [40] mitigates this quadratic cost, it treats all spatial locations uniformly, hindering spatially-adaptive longrange aggregation. Meanwhile, although feed-forward networks (FFNs) scale linearly, materializing their large expanded HR features incurs heavy memory traffic not reflected by MACs. For plain FFN, kernel fusion [9, 23] avoids this materialization, yielding up to 5.05 inference speedup at identical MACs  (Table 9)  . Still, widely used 1 Convolutional FFNs (ConvFFNs)1 apply depthwise convolution (DWC) to expanded features, introducing cross-pixel dependencies that complicate such fusion. Together, the computational and memory overheads of these two core operators pose substantial challenge to efficient HR processing. This raises central question: Can we substantially reduce the overheads of processing HR features while fully leveraging the benefits of multi-scale architecture? To answer this question, we propose High-resolution Global-Local Restoration (HiGLR), multi-scale restoration network guided by stage-wise attention analysis. At the finest-scale stage, we observe attention readout redundancy: the residual attention outputs beyond uniform pooling heavily overlap across spatial queries  (Table 1)  , motivating cheaper spatial mixing with learned, input-independent kernels, as supported by our replacement ablation (Sec. 8). Furthermore, at the intermediate resolution stages, attention is more concentrated on subset of keys, motivating sparse query-key interactions. Lastly, at the coarsest stage, the smaller token count makes dense attention affordable [19]. At intermediate resolution stages, we further observe routing redundancy: neighboring queries can share keyselection indices for sparse attention with only modest reduction in retained attention mass under small fixed budget  (Table 1)  . This motivates sharing routing decisions among neighboring queries [10, 46] in block-sparse attention [11, 14, 20], yielding up to 5.25 attention speedup at the intermediate stages. Still, attending to many blocks remains costly, while selecting only few leaves the remaining regions unaggregated. We therefore propose BlockRouted Hybrid Attention (BRHA), which combines dense attention over compressed block summaries with sharedrouting sparse attention over value residuals relative to these summaries. This hybrid design allows sparse attention to focus on small subset of blocks while maintaining global coverage through compressed block summaries. Beyond attention, to resolve the HR memory bottleneck in ConvFFNs, we exploit spatial redundancy to decouple spatial mixing from nonlinear feature expansion. Specifically, across two pretrained AIO-IR models [7, 38], we observe that restoration quality is far less sensitive to outputrank reduction in spatial interaction than in intra-pixel nonlinearity  (Fig. 3)  . Motivated by this asymmetry, we propose the Dual-Space Feed-Forward Network (DSFFN), which performs spatial mixing in compact space and injects the resulting spatial context into expanded features for pointwise nonlinear transformation. Confining cross-pixel dependencies to the compact space keeps the expanded-space operations pointwise, facilitating memory-efficient kernel fusion, especially as the feature expansion ratio increases. Combining these designs, HiGLR achieves state-of-theart performance on AIO-3, AIO-5, and CDD-11 with only 1In this paper, we refer to Restormers [40] GDFN as ConvFFN. 7M parameters, while reducing inference latency by 76.4% and peak GPU memory by 65.8% compared with CEAIR-S  (Table 4)  . Extensive ablations further support our stage-wise design choices and demonstrate the benefits of residual-based hybrid attention and decoupled spatial mixing, while characterizing their qualityefficiency trade-offs. Overall, our contributions are summarized as follows: Resolution-Aware Architecture via Redundancy Analysis: We uncover per-query readout, spatial keyrouting, and FFN spatial-rank redundancies, and introduce HiGLR to address HR compute and memory bottlenecks without sacrificing multi-scale representations. Block-Routed Hybrid Attention (BRHA): We propose an I/O-aware hybrid attention mechanism that shares routing indices across neighboring queries and couples dense attention over block summaries with block-sparse attention over on-the-fly value residuals. Dual-Space Feed-Forward Network (DSFFN): We confine depthwise spatial mixing to compact subspace while keeping expanded nonlinear transformations purely pointwise, enabling end-to-end kernel fusion that drastically reduces memory traffic at HR features. 2. Related Work Efficient Image Restoration and All-in-One Restoration. Efficient restoration backbones [5, 40] and degradationadaptive models [13, 18, 25, 28, 33, 38] have advanced the qualityefficiency trade-off in IR and AIO-IR. For example, Restormer [40] replaces spatial attention with channel attention to reduce HR costs, while MoCE-IR [38] adapts processing capacity through experts of different complexities. However, processing large HR feature maps remains costly: spatial attention requires many token interactions, while expanded FFN activations incur substantial memory traffic. We address these complementary costs through resolutionaware operator allocation, combining compact spatial mixing at full resolution with sparse global aggregation at intermediate stages. Sparse and Hybrid Attention Methods. Sparse selfattention offers way to reduce the computation and memory costs of dense attention [32] while retaining contentadaptive access to distant For example, BiFormer [46] routes queries to selected key regions, while SemanIR [26] retrieves semantically related keys and shares their indices across layers. However, aggressive selection limits the spatial information directly available to each query, making global context harder to retain under small budget. Hybrid methods address this limitation through compressed-context branches [36] or low-rank attention approximations [3]. In contrast, our BRHA exploits the spatial structure of visual features through value residualization: coarse attention aggregates block summaries globally, tokens. 2 Figure 2. Overview of HiGLR. (a) The multi-scale architecture and (b) its main block use DSFFN at all scales, BRHA at intermediate resolutions, and dense self-attention at the coarsest scale. (c) DSFFN decouples compact spatial mixing from expanded pointwise transformations. (d) BRHA combines coarse global attention with block-sparse residual attention. while sparse fine attention aggregates deviations within selected blocks. Efficient FFNs and Spatial Mixing Methods. ConvFFNs [40] are widely used in IR to enrich per-token representations with local spatial context [7, 13, 25, 38]. In such designs, materializing expanded HR features incurs substantial memory traffic, while cross-pixel dependencies complicate kernel fusion [8]. Some prior designs place spatial convolution before channel expansion [4, 22] or apply it to only subset of expanded channels [45]. These changes in the placement or channel scope of spatial mixing do not by themselves eliminate the materialization of expanded FFN features. In contrast, our DSFFN explicitly targets this objective through kernel fusion, confining spatial mixing to compact space whose width is independent of both the input and expanded widths while keeping expanded nonlinear transformations pointwise. 3. Proposed Methods 3.1. Overall Architecture As shown in Fig. 2 (a), HiGLR adopts four-stage UNet architecture [29], following the multi-scale design commonly used in AIO-IR [25, 38]. An input convolution maps the degraded image ILQ RHW 3 to shallow features, which the encoder processes at resolutions from to 8 . Each encoder and decoder stage stacks main blocks (Fig. 2 (b)) that use DSFFN for local mixing and stage-specific global mixer BRHA at the two intermediate scales, dense self-attention at the coarsest scale, and no global mixer at the finest scale. 8 At the two intermediate scales, degradation extractors map the incoming encoder features to degradation feature maps. Their block-wise descriptors condition BRHA in both the encoder and the corresponding decoder stage, adapting block scores to the input degradation. The two degradation feature maps are globally average-pooled and concatenated, then fed to an auxiliary degradation classifier trained with cross-entropy supervision. The classifier supervises the extractors during training; restoration at inference uses their descriptors without requiring class predictions or degradation labels. The decoder progressively upsamples features and combines them with same-resolution encoder features through additive skip connections. Full-resolution refinement aggregates intermediate features through dense connections [44], and an output convolution produces the restored image IHQ RHW 3. Throughout, X, RHsWsCs denote modules input and output at stage s, with defined before the enclosing skip connection. We omit the stage subscript when clear from context. 3.2. Sparsity and Redundancy in Self-Attention Stage-dependent attention pattern. Self-attention effectively captures long-range dependencies, but its quadratic complexity poses severe computational bottleneck on HR feature maps. Sparse attention [10, 11, 14, 20] offers promising way to reduce this cost, but its suitability depends on how strongly attention mass is concentrated on small subset of keys. Notably, as shown in Table 1, evaluating fixed 25% key-token budget, query-wise key selection 3 retains 90.7% and 85.6% of the attention mass at the two intermediate stages, compared with 80.2% at the coarsest stage and only 58.7% at full resolution. This high concentration supports sparse fine-grained aggregation at intermediate resolutions, whereas the reduced token count makes dense attention directly affordable at the coarsest stage. Per-query readout redundancy at full resolution. At full resolution, attention is not only diffuse (58.7% retained mass), but its residual output beyond uniform pooling is largely shared across spatial queries (92.87%; Table 1). Similar cross-query redundancy has also been reported in the global context features produced by non-local networks [2]. This high readout redundancy indicates limited spatial differentiation on average across the two SA layers, despite costly query-wise aggregation (59.86 ms). Together with global context aggregation at lower resolutions, this observation motivates investigating whether input-independent local mixing can replace lightweight, costly full-resolution attention. Our replacement experiment supports this design choice, improving average PSNR by 0.39 dB (Sec. 8). Spatial redundancy in key routing. Even with concentrated attention at intermediate stages, independently selecting keys for every spatial query incurs substantial routing overhead. Exploiting spatial correlations among neighboring features, we compare individual and block-shared routing under the same 25% key-token budget. Sharing key indices within 8 8 query blocks retains 88.0% and 79.6% of the attention mass at the two intermediate stages, only 2.7%p and 6.0%p below individual routing, respectively. Neighboring queries can thus share routing decisions with minimal loss in retained attention mass, yielding up to 5.25 attention speedup at the intermediate stages, as shown in Table 5. 3.3. Block-Routed Hybrid Attention Although our preliminary analyses in Sec. 3.2 suggest the potential for sparse attention at intermediate stages, retaining most of the attention mass with sparse attention alone requires substantial key budget; the evaluated 25% budget still entails 2/4 querykey interactions for tokens. More aggressive sparsification reduces this cost, but restricts fine-grained interactions to fewer spatial regions. We therefore propose BRHA, which combines dense aggregation of learned summaries from all blocks with sparse aggregation of token-wise residuals within selected blocks, using shared key and value projections. To exploit spatial redundancy in routing, queries within the same block share the selected key-block indices. Experiments In this section, we evaluate HiGLRs restoration quality, efficiency, and key design choices. Implementation and training details are provided in Sections 10 and 11. 4.1. Quantitative Results To measure restoration across task mixtures and compound degradations, we compare HiGLR with representative AIOIR methods [7, 13, 27, 33, 38] on AIO-3 [18], AIO-5 [33], and CDD-11 [12], reporting PSNR and SSIM measured in the RGB color space following previous work [33]. On AIO-3 and AIO-5, HiGLR averages 33.14 and 31.30 dB, exceeding CEA-IR by 0.07 and 0.17 dB with 7M versus 22M parameters  (Table 3)  . On CDD-11, HiGLR averages 31.56 dB, 1.02 dB above BioIR-B, with the highest PSNR and SSIM in all eleven conditions  (Table 2)  . These results demonstrate the superior performance of HiGLR and highlight the importance of processing HR features. 4.2. Efficiency Comparison To measure inference speed and memory efficiency, we compare latency, peak GPU memory, and DRAM traffic against representative AIO-IR methods [7, 13, 27, 33, 38]. Following prior methods, we use FP32 precision by default, with BF16 selectively employed only for attention core computations [8]. We measure DRAM traffic as total reads and writes using NVIDIA Nsight Compute (NCU). At 512 512 on an RTX 4090, HiGLR requires only 22.64 ms and 294.9 MiB of peak allocated memory, running 3.93 faster with 79.0% lower peak memory than BioIR-B  (Table 4)  . Overall Network Architecture Table 13 summarizes the encoder and decoder at each resolution. The encoder traverses stages 14, with stage 4 containing only encoder blocks, and the decoder traverses stages 31. Between stages, downsampling uses 2 2 convolutions with stride 2, and upsampling uses 1 1 convolutions followed by 2 pixel shuffle. All DSFFNs use expansion ratio γ = 3 and 3 3 depthwise convolutions, with spatial widths = [16, 16, 32, 64] at stages 14. Attention uses 64 channels per head, giving one, two, and four heads at stages 2, 3, and 4, respectively. Decoder stage 1 uses dense connections, as detailed in Section 10.5. At the two intermediate stages, degradation extractors consist of 33 convolutions that produce feature maps whose block-wise descriptors condition BRHA. As shown in Figure 6, the globally pooled features from both stages are concatenated and passed to an auxiliary classifier trained with cross-entropy supervision. 10.2. K-Smoothing and Numerical Precision We accelerate dense attention with FlashAttention-2 [6], whose CUDA backend requires FP16/BF16 inputs. Since low-precision training can degrade restoration quality [9], we retain FP32 QKV projections, consistent with prior restoration implementations [3, 4, 13, 20, 26]. When di14 rectly casting these projections to BF16 for attention, we observe excessively large query and key norms in certain layers. Related low-bit attention studies also identify Q/K outliers as source of numerical sensitivity [22, 23]. Following these studies, we apply K-smoothing. Technically, we project keys and subtract their spatial mean in FP32 before casting them to BF16. On CDD-11 ablation, Ksmoothing improves PSNR from 30.21 to 30.37 dB. In particularly affected dense attention head, the mean pertoken query and key norms are 81.4% and 52.5% lower, respectively (before key mean subtraction), while normalized attention entropy increases from 0.028 to 0.559. 10.3. Efficient BRHA Implementation Our Triton [16] inference implementation computes routing and coarse aggregation in separate tiled passes without storing the full block-score matrix S. The routing pass merges tile-local top-kr candidates while accumulating logsum-exp statistics over all remote blocks. These statistics normalize the selected log gates over all remote blocks, as required by Eq. (4); the query block itself is included separately with zero log gate. The resulting block indices and gates are stored for fine attention. The coarse pass recomputes the score tiles and uses online softmax to accumulate Oc over all block summaries. In our RTX 4090 measurements, recomputing the scores yielded slightly lower end-to-end latency and peak allocated memory than storing them. Fine attention then processes each query block using the selected-block list shared by its queries. For each selected block, the kernel loads its keys and values, subtracting the block summary from the values to avoid allocating separate token-resolution residual-value tensor. The kernel adds the relative position bias and the block log gate to the toplies GELU and sigmoid gating, and immediately accumulates the gated result through Wo into the C-channel output. Thus, no full-image buffers are allocated for Z, G, Ws(T ), or the gated activations. The kernel scales the residual branch by its learned weight and adds the input features before writing the output. At lower-resolution stages, the compact projection Wr, RMSNorm, and GELU are computed before separate depthwise convolution, with the R-channel intermediate features stored in global memory. At full resolution, we further reduce memory traffic by fusing this path into the same kernel, using one-pixel halos and recomputing compact features in overlapping tile borders to avoid full-image buffers for both the pre-convolution features and . During training, we retain the input and compact-path features but do not cache expanded activations for backward. The backward pass recomputes the expanded pointwise operations from these saved tensors, while reusing the compact projection and depthwise-convolution results. Recomputed gated activations and value/gate gradients are temporarily materialized for weight-gradient GEMMs. 10.5. We therefore use 16 DSFFNs at the decoder 1 stage and aggregate intermediate features through dense connections [25], as illustrated in Figure 8. Full Quantitative Results To assess restoration performance across diverse degradation types, we report the full per-task comparisons on AIO3 and AIO-5 in Tables 15 and 16, respectively. On AIO-3, HiGLR achieves the highest average PSNR of 33.14 dB, exceeding CEA-IR by 0.07 dB. Moreover, on AIO-5, which additionally includes deblurring and low-light enhancement, HiGLR achieves the highest average PSNR and SSIM of 31.30 dB and 0.926, respectively. Together, these results support HiGLRs ability to handle diverse restoration tasks within only 7M parameters, achieving higher average PSNR on both benchmarks than the 22M-parameter CEA-IR. 14. We examine the number of stages, the remote-block budget across attention variants, the choice of global operator at each stage, and the role of degradation conditioning and its auxiliary loss. 14.1. Moreover, the attention statistics in Section 7 suggest why BRHA can remain effective even at the bottleneck of shallower model. In the three-stage encoder, neighboring queries at H/4 can share small set of keys and still retain most of their attention mass  (Table 10)  . Consistent with this observation, the three-stage restoration model achieves higher PSNR with BRHA at H/4 than with dense attention there. In the five-stage model, extending BRHA all the way to H/16 lowers PSNR, suggesting that access to keys outside the shared set is useful at this coarser scale. The best five-stage result therefore comes from reserving dense attention for H/16. Switching one stage earlier, at H/8, makes the model faster but sacrifices restoration quality. 14.2. Stage-wise Global Mixers With the four-stage hierarchy fixed, we ask whether global mixer would complement the local DSFFNs at full resolution and whether BRHA could replace dense attention at the bottleneck  (Table 18)  . At full resolution, the residual readout of dense spatial attention is largely shared across queries  (Table 10)  , suggesting limited benefit from computing separate spatial readout for every query. MDTA offers another efficient way to incorporate global context at this scale by mixing channels. Yet local DSFFNs perform on par with MDTA in the AIO-5 replacement study  (Table 11)  , and the CDD-11 variant that adds MDTA to the Stage 1 encoder shows no PSNR gain over HiGLR. These observations support keeping the finest stage local and relying on coarser stages for global context. At the bottleneck, we ask whether BRHA can replace dense self-attention without sacrificing restoration quality. In the four-stage encoder, block-wise routing with fixed 25% key budget leaves more attention mass outside the selected set at H/8 than at H/2 or H/4  (Table 10)  . Consistent with this observation, replacing dense attention with BRHA at H/8 lowers CDD-11 PSNR  (Table 18)  . Extending BRHA to the H/16 bottleneck of the five-stage model has the same effect  (Table 17)  . Also note that, at H/8, the token count is small enough that dense attention runs faster per module than BRHA on 512512 inputs  (Table 5)  . Thus, keeping dense attention at the four-stage bottleneck favors both restoration quality and inference speed at that scale. 14.3. Comparisons on Attention Variants Reducing the remote-block budget kr limits the regions that fine attention can sample, while coarse attention still aggregates information from the entire image. To test whether this global context helps preserve restoration quality at small budgets, we vary kr at inference on CDD11 with each models weights fixed. We compare Sparseonly, which attends directly to values in the selected blocks, with two hybrid variants that combine dense attention over pooled block values with sparse attention over residual token values. The two hybrid variants differ in whether the routing scores also gate fine attention. In full BRHA, this log gate allows the restoration loss to update the scores used for block selection during training. When the budget falls from 16 remote blocks to one, Log-gate OFF loses less PSNR than Sparse-only, and full BRHA loses less than half as much as Sparse-only (Figure 9 (a)). This ordering suggests that the coarse path preserves context from blocks omitted by fine attention and that learning the routing scores through the log gate further improves robustness to smaller budget. The advantage also holds in absolute PSNR. Log-gate OFF with six remote blocks and full BRHA with just one both outperform Sparse-only attending to approximately 25% of the key/value blocks (Figure 9 (b)). Notably, the coarse path can cover all blocks efficiently because it reuses the routing scores to weight the pooled values.
